name: VI Peel

angle.text: It is a branded medium peel marketed for acne, pigment, sun damage and fine lines across skin tones. Published data are a few small studies.

summary: A branded TCA-phenol-salicylic medium peel marketed for all skin tones; published data are a few small studies.
note: Ingredient details and history rest largely on manufacturer-derived information.
currentQuick:
The VI Peel is a branded medium-depth peel from the Vitality Institute, combining acids, phenol, tretinoin and vitamin C. It is marketed for acne, pigment, sun damage and scars.
Published research is limited to small studies such as a 30-patient peel-plus-neurotoxin study.
How it works: The blend causes controlled exfoliation of the epidermis and upper dermis, according to the company-derived description.
Risks and caveats: Peel side effects include redness, peeling and pigment change; product-specific safety data are sparse.
deepLead:
The VI Peel is a branded medium-depth chemical peel made by the Vitality Institute. According to Grokipedia, an AI-generated reference, it blends trichloroacetic acid, phenol, salicylic acid, tretinoin and vitamin C, and is marketed for acne, pigmentation, sun damage, acne scarring, melasma and fine lines for all Fitzpatrick skin types.
The same source says the company was founded by emergency physician Abdala Khalil, who developed an initial formulation for his daughter's cystic acne, with a commercial launch around 2005 to 2006 and a body formulation in 2022. These history details come from a single unverified source.
Published research is limited: a 2024 study of 30 patients examined same-day VI Peel and neurotoxin treatment. Exact ingredient ratios are described as proprietary.

name: Obagi Blue Peel

angle.text: It is a branded TCA peel designed to be deeper than superficial peels while keeping depth predictable. Its published record is thin, including a 1999 paper describing the standardized method.

summary: A branded, standardized TCA medium-depth peel with a thin published record.
note: Evidence is limited to a procedure description and small comparisons.
currentQuick:
The Obagi Blue Peel is a branded TCA-based medium peel. A 1999 paper described it as a standardized method with depth control.
Few studies exist beyond that and a hand-rejuvenation comparison.
How it works: TCA causes controlled injury to the epidermis and upper dermis, after which skin sheds and renews.
Risks and caveats: Medium peels carry risks of pigment change, prolonged redness and scarring.
deepLead:
The Obagi Blue Peel is a branded TCA-based medium-depth chemical peel. A 1999 Dermatologic Surgery paper described a standardized TCA-based blue peel intended to be deeper than superficial exfoliating peels while offering depth control, addressing the observation that TCA peel results vary with technique and patient selection.
Published studies are few: a 2002 comparison of Er:YAG laser and Blue Peel for photoaged hands, a 2006 paper on performing the peel faster and less expensively, and a 2000 letter commenting on the technique.

name: PCA Peel

angle.text: It is a line of professional chemical peels sold by PCA Skin for general skin renewal and pigment concerns. The claims come from the manufacturer and independent published trials were not found.

summary: A branded professional peel line from PCA Skin; manufacturer claims are not backed by independent published trials.
note: Most information comes from the company's own materials.
currentQuick:
PCA Peel is a brand of professional chemical peels from PCA Skin, owned by Colgate-Palmolive since 2018. Its signature peel is described as a modified Jessner's formula.
The company reports clinical testing but no independent published trials were found.
How it works: Acid blends cause controlled superficial exfoliation, according to the company.
Risks and caveats: Peels in general can cause irritation, burning and peeling; consumer reviews cited in one source mention these.
deepLead:
PCA Peel is a line of professional chemical peels sold by the skincare company PCA Skin. According to a summary of the company's own materials, the brand was founded in 1990 and in 2017 Colgate-Palmolive announced it would acquire PCA Skin, a deal completed in January 2018.
The flagship product is described by the company as a modified, enhanced Jessner's peel combining lactic, salicylic, kojic and citric acids with resorcinol, marketed as self-neutralizing, with TCA-and-lactic-acid blends in the wider range. The entry in this wiki was added as a branded TCA, lactic and salicylic peel.
The company's claims (such as being the leading peel brand among estheticians and more than one million peels performed yearly) come from its own materials and have not been independently verified in the sources reviewed. No independent clinical studies of the PCA Peel were found.

name: Cosmelan peel

angle.text: It is used for melasma, dark marks and sun spots in a clinic mask phase followed by months of home care. Claims come from the manufacturer; no published trials were found.

summary: A mesoestetic depigmenting mask-and-cream protocol for melasma and spots; claims come from the manufacturer and no published trials were found.
note: Rebound pigmentation and irritation are discussed by the company, who stress sun protection; no independent studies found.
currentQuick:
Cosmelan is a professional depigmentation treatment from mesoestetic: a mask applied in clinic, then months of home cream and sunscreen. It is aimed at melasma and other pigment.
No published trials were found; information comes from the maker.
How it works: The company says it removes existing melanin deposits and regulates melanocyte activity.
Risks and caveats: Contraindications listed by the maker include pregnancy, isotretinoin use and vitiligo history; the company stresses sunscreen to avoid rebound pigmentation.
deepLead:
Cosmelan is a professional depigmenting treatment developed by the Spanish company mesoestetic, marketed for melasma, post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation, solar lentigines and freckles. According to Grokipedia, an AI-generated reference drawing on company material, it has two phases: an in-clinic mask left on for several hours, followed by roughly six months of home cream and sun protection.
The company states it corrects existing spots and regulates melanin production, and is suitable for all phototypes; these are manufacturer claims. No peer-reviewed trials of Cosmelan were found in the sources reviewed.

name: Dermamelan

angle.text: Appearance communities discuss it as a way to even out skin tone and fade melasma. Support is limited to one small pilot study.

summary: A professional non-hydroquinone depigmenting treatment for melasma, backed by one small pilot study.
note: Only a single 2011 pilot study was found; depigmenting treatments can cause irritation and should be professionally supervised according to dermatology guidance generally.
currentQuick:
Dermamelan is a depigmenting treatment marketed for melasma and uneven pigmentation. It is described in the literature as a non-hydroquinone bleaching formulation.
The published evidence is limited to one small pilot study from 2011 that used confocal microscopy to examine the skin.
How it works: It is intended to reduce melanin deposits in the skin; the available source describes it as an alternative to hydroquinone, the most widely used depigmenting agent.
Risks and caveats: Safety was assessed in the pilot study, but larger trials have not been identified, so the full adverse-effect profile is not documented in the sources reviewed.
deepLead:
Dermamelan is the name of a depigmenting (skin-lightening) treatment marketed for melasma and other pigmentation, described in the literature as a non-hydroquinone bleaching formulation . It is a professional aesthetic treatment rather than a chemical peel in the classical sense, and it is discussed in appearance communities as a way to even out skin tone.
Published evidence is very thin. A pilot study published in 2011 used reflectance confocal microscopy, an in vivo imaging technique, to assess the efficacy and safety of a new non-hydroquinone formulation called Dermamelan for melasma, motivated by the observation that treatment of melasma with the common agent hydroquinone remains unsatisfactory . No larger trials appear among the available sources.

name: Retinol peel (Retinoic acid peel)

angle.text: It is used for photoaging, scars, wrinkles and pigment. A few small trials exist for photoaging and acanthosis nigricans, with no consensus protocol.

summary: A clinic-applied tretinoin peel with a few small trials in photoaging and acanthosis nigricans but no consensus protocol.
note: Reviewers note a lack of consensus; irritation, redness and pigment changes are reported peel risks.
currentQuick:
A retinoic acid peel applies a tretinoin solution in a clinic, usually at around 5% strength in trials, to treat photoaging, melasma and similar concerns.
Research includes a placebo-controlled photoaging trial and laser comparisons in acanthosis nigricans, though a review describes the field as lacking consensus.
How it works: Tretinoin is a retinoid used topically for acne, melasma, scars and aging; as a peel it is applied in higher concentrations to cause a controlled superficial exfoliation.
Risks and caveats: General peel risks include stinging, redness, dryness and pigment changes, rising with depth.
deepLead:
A retinoic acid (tretinoin) peel is a superficial chemical peel in which a retinoid solution, often at 5% concentration in studies, is applied to the skin in a clinic and later washed off or left to act . A review describes it as a superficial peeling frequently performed in dermatological clinics in Brazil, with a first study on melasma published in 2001 . Wikipedia describes retinoic acid peels as deeper than alpha-hydroxy acid peels, used for scars, wrinkles and pigment, and often preceded by a Jessner's peel .
Evidence includes a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial in facial photoaging and comparative trials in acanthosis nigricans . A critical review states that studies have reported applicability with reasonable methodology but without a consistent scientific background or consensus .

name: Salicylic acid peel

angle.text: It is the superficial peel most often used for acne and pigmentation. Small comparative studies support its acne use.

summary: The oil-soluble BHA peel most often studied for acne, supported by small comparative studies.
note: Superficial peels commonly cause stinging, redness and dryness.
currentQuick:
A salicylic acid peel uses a beta-hydroxy acid at roughly 20 to 30% to exfoliate the skin, mainly for acne and some pigmentation.
Evidence is mostly small studies and trial registrations comparing it with other peels.
How it works: Wikipedia describes salicylic acid as antibacterial, anti-inflammatory and oil-soluble, which is why it is associated with acne-prone skin.
Risks and caveats: Light peels commonly cause stinging, redness, irritation and dryness; deeper peels carry higher complication risks such as pigment change.
deepLead:
A salicylic acid peel is a superficial chemical peel using salicylic acid, a beta-hydroxy acid (BHA), commonly at 20 to 30% in clinical studies and used mainly for acne and pigmentation . Wikipedia describes salicylic acid as antibacterial and anti-inflammatory and increasingly preferred over AHAs because it is oil-soluble, though the oil-solubility claim is flagged there as needing a citation .
Published evidence consists mostly of small comparative studies and registered trials. A 2014 study compared 50% pyruvic and 30% salicylic peels on sebum secretion in 20 people with acne .

name: Glycolic acid peel

angle.text: It is the most widely studied AHA peel, used for melasma, dark under-eyes, acne scars and fine lines. Studies are mostly small.

summary: The most widely studied AHA peel, tested in melasma, periorbital darkening and acne scars in mostly small studies.
note: Stinging, redness and dryness are common; home kits have been associated with injury.
currentQuick:
A glycolic acid peel exfoliates the skin using an alpha-hydroxy acid and is used for pigmentation, acne scars and general texture.
It has the largest body of small comparative studies among the common peels, though many are from single centers.
How it works: It is a mild superficial peel that loosens the outer skin layers, which then shed.
Risks and caveats: Common effects are stinging, redness, irritation and dryness; pigment change is among reported complications, and Wikipedia notes weak home kits can cause injury and scarring.
deepLead:
A glycolic acid peel is a superficial chemical peel using glycolic acid, an alpha-hydroxy acid. Alpha hydroxy acids (AHAs) are described by Wikipedia as the mildest peels, used for fine wrinkles, dryness, uneven pigment and acne . One article calls it one of the most versatile agents in melasma treatment .
Studies in Indian and other patient groups have examined glycolic peels, at concentrations such as 20% or 30%, for melasma, periorbital melanosis and acne scars, often alone against other peels or combined with other agents .

name: Lactic acid peel

angle.text: It is used as a gentle peel for dark under-eye circles and melasma. A few small comparisons exist.

summary: A mild AHA peel studied in a few small comparisons for periorbital darkening and melasma.
note: Evidence comes from a few small comparative studies.
currentQuick:
A lactic acid peel is a mild alpha-hydroxy acid peel used for pigmentation such as melasma and dark under-eye skin.
Published work is a handful of small studies comparing it with glycolic and other peels.
How it works: Like other AHA peels it loosens and removes outer skin layers in a controlled superficial way.
Risks and caveats: Light peels commonly cause stinging, redness, irritation and dryness; deeper or stronger peels carry higher complication risk.
deepLead:
A lactic acid peel is a superficial chemical peel using lactic acid, an alpha-hydroxy acid. Alpha hydroxy acids (AHAs) are described by Wikipedia as the mildest peels, used for fine wrinkles, dryness, uneven pigment and acne . Studies have used it at 15% for periorbital melanosis  and at 92% for epidermal melasma .
Evidence is limited to a few comparative studies, mostly in Indian patients, usually comparing lactic acid against glycolic or trichloroacetic acid peels .

name: Mandelic acid peel

angle.text: It is promoted as a gentle peel for people across age groups and skin tones. Only two small studies stand behind it.

summary: A gentle AHA peel with only two small studies behind it.
note: Very limited published evidence.
currentQuick:
A mandelic acid peel is a mild alpha-hydroxy acid peel used for acne-prone and sensitive or mature skin.
Only two small published studies were found: one on sebum in older women and one on adult acne in combination with salicylic acid.
How it works: It is a superficial exfoliating peel; researchers have measured its effect on sebum secretion.
Risks and caveats: Authors of the sebum study describe it as mild with no side effects reported; light peels generally can cause stinging, redness and dryness.
deepLead:
A mandelic acid peel uses mandelic acid, an alpha-hydroxy acid described as gentle in the aesthetic literature, which notes azelaic and mandelic peels are commonly used across age groups . Wikipedia's chemical peel article does not discuss mandelic acid specifically .
Published evidence is limited to a 2013 sebum study in mature women and a 2022 acne trial using a combined salicylic and mandelic peel .

name: Pyruvic acid peel

angle.text: Users book pyruvic acid peels to clear active acne and refresh dull, congested skin. It is a keratolytic peel described mainly for acne vulgaris, and the evidence for that use is a handful of small studies.

summary: A clinic-applied superficial acne peel using an alpha-keto acid; evidence is a handful of small studies.
note: Evidence base is very small; all peels carry risk of irritation and pigment change.
currentQuick:
Pyruvic acid peels are superficial chemical peels applied in a clinic, mostly studied for acne.
The published evidence is thin: a small 2014 comparison with salicylic acid peels in 20 acne patients is the main study found.
How it works: Pyruvic acid is a keratolytic alpha-keto acid that loosens the outer skin layers so they shed, which is how peels are described to work.
Risks and caveats: Peels in general can cause redness, photosensitivity, pigment change and, rarely, scarring. Pyruvic acid peels are applied by clinicians.
deepLead:
A pyruvic acid peel is a superficial chemical peel that uses pyruvic acid, an alpha-keto acid, applied to the skin by a clinician to loosen and shed the outer layers. It is described in dermatology literature as a keratolytic peel used mainly in acne vulgaris.
Published evidence is small. One comparison of 50% pyruvic acid and 30% salicylic acid peels in 20 patients with acne measured effects on facial sebum secretion. Chemical peels in general are described as causing a controlled injury that makes the skin peel, with risks including prolonged redness, pigment change and scarring.

name: Phenol-croton oil peel

chain: Deep peel removes damaged skin layers
angle.text: The phenol-croton oil peel is the classic deep resurfacing treatment for wrinkles and skin tightening, with the smoother, tighter result visible once healing is complete. It has been used since the 1962 Baker-Gordon formula, and gentler low-phenol versions are now used as well.

summary: The classic deep surgical-grade peel for wrinkles and tightening, now used in gentler low-phenol versions.
note: Deep peel done by physicians; pigment loss, scarring and prolonged recovery are documented.
currentQuick:
A phenol-croton oil peel is a deep chemical peel used for wrinkles and skin tightening. The classic 1962 Baker-Gordon formula has largely been replaced by lower-concentration versions.
Evidence is mostly surgeon case series, formula studies and lab work rather than randomized trials.
How it works: Croton oil is reported to be the main active peeling agent, with phenol acting as a carrier at lower concentrations; the peel injures the skin deeply and is followed by collagen remodeling.
Risks and caveats: Deeper peels carry more complications: prolonged redness, pigment change, atrophy and scarring. They are performed by physicians, often with sedation.
deepLead:
The phenol-croton oil peel is a deep chemical peel used for facial resurfacing, wrinkle reduction and skin tightening. The classic Baker-Gordon formula, published in 1962, was long considered the standard for deep facial resurfacing.
Reviews report that classical high-phenol formulas have largely been replaced by formulas with lower phenol and croton oil concentrations, which are described as having a better safety profile and more natural results, without the complete pigment loss once typical of deep peels. Research by plastic surgeon Gregory Hetter argued that croton oil, rather than phenol, is the peel's active ingredient.

name: Chemical reconstruction of skin scars

chain: Strong TCA placed in scar base
Scar floor rebuilds with new collagen
angle.text: People with ice-pick and other atrophic acne scars use CROSS to make individual scars shallower without treating the whole face. It has been studied in small trials for exactly this use.

summary: Spot-applying strong TCA acid into individual acne scars; studied in small trials.
note: Clinician procedure; sources found are thin.
currentQuick:
CROSS places a strong TCA solution into individual depressed scars, mainly acne scars, instead of peeling the whole face.
Only small trial registrations were found in the sources reviewed.
How it works: The acid is said to trigger a focal wound-healing response in the scar base.
Risks and caveats: TCA peels can cause redness, pigment change and scarring. The technique is performed by clinicians.
deepLead:
Chemical reconstruction of skin scars (CROSS) is a focal technique in which a high-concentration trichloroacetic acid (TCA) solution is applied to the base of individual atrophic scars, such as ice-pick acne scars, rather than to the whole face.
Evidence in the sources reviewed is limited to small registered trials. Wikipedia lists TCA as a medium-depth peel agent used in office settings.

name: Skinvive

angle.text: Skinvive is promoted for a hydrated, glassy glow and smoother texture rather than added volume. Users choose it as a skin-quality treatment, and the evidence for that use is early-stage.

summary: Microdroplet hyaluronic acid injected into the skin for texture and glow; early-stage evidence.
note: Injectable medical procedure; trial evidence is recent and small.
currentQuick:
Skinvive is an Allergan hyaluronic acid product injected into the skin to improve skin quality such as hydration and fine lines, not volume.
Published evidence is small and recent, including a 25-person split-face trial combined with botulinum toxin.
How it works: Hyaluronic acid binds water in skin; here it is placed in many tiny droplets within the skin.
Risks and caveats: Filler injections can cause redness, swelling, bruising and, less commonly, granulomas. It is a clinician-administered product.
deepLead:
Skinvive (Juvederm Volite VYC-12) is a hyaluronic acid injectable made by Allergan that is placed in the skin itself in many small microdroplets to improve skin quality, rather than to add volume. It belongs to the Juvederm range of hyaluronic acid products.
Evidence found is limited to a 2025 split-face trial of combined botulinum toxin and Skinvive and a handful of manufacturer-linked registered trials, including one of Volite for neck lines.

name: Profhilo Structura

chain: HA placed in superficial fat compartments
angle.text: Profhilo Structura is marketed to restore cheek and facial volume, particularly in the lateral cheek, using a hybrid hyaluronic acid. People use it for a fuller, lifted midface, and the evidence for that use so far is small case series.

summary: A high-concentration hybrid hyaluronic acid injectable aimed at restoring cheek and facial fat volume, backed so far by small case series.
note: Evidence is small studies; large registered trial has no published results yet.
currentQuick:
Profhilo Structura is a hybrid hyaluronic acid product from IBSA that is injected by a clinician into superficial facial fat layers, mainly the cheeks, to restore volume and contour.
Published data so far consist of a 22-person case series, an observational pilot study and lab comparisons, with a 164-person trial still registered as ongoing.
How it works: It combines high- and low-molecular-weight hyaluronic acid into stable complexes using the NAHYCO process, without chemical cross-linking. Authors propose it may influence fat tissue homeostasis, though this is a hypothesis.
Risks and caveats: Risks described for injectable HA generally include bruising, swelling and injection-site reactions. Product-specific safety data are limited to small studies, and it is administered only by trained clinicians.
deepLead:
Profhilo Structura is an injectable hyaluronic acid (HA) product made by IBSA Farmaceutici, marketed as a medical device for restoring facial volume and contour, particularly in superficial fat compartments of the face such as the lateral cheek. It is a variant of the original Profhilo "skin remodelling" product and uses the same patented NAHYCO hybrid technology, which combines high- and low-molecular-weight HA into thermally stabilised complexes without chemical cross-linking.
In a published case series, the product delivered 45 mg each of high-molecular-weight (about 1400 kDa) and low-molecular-weight (about 100 kDa) HA in a 2 mL syringe, and was placed with a cannula into the superficial fat compartment of each hemiface. Its manufacturer-linked and independent clinicians describe it as a way to address the loss of facial fat volume associated with ageing, rather than as a conventional bolus filler.
Published evidence is limited to a small case series, an observational pilot study, laboratory comparisons with other HA fillers and a registered ongoing trial. These report improvements in clinician- and patient-rated measures, but they are small, uncontrolled and, in several cases, linked to the manufacturer.

name: Profhilo Body

chain: Hybrid HA injected into body skin
angle.text: Profhilo Body is used to improve laxity and roughness of body skin such as the upper inner arms and backs of the hands. The evidence for that use is small single-arm trials.

summary: A hybrid hyaluronic acid skin booster for body skin laxity, studied so far in small single-arm trials.
note: Evidence limited to small uncontrolled studies and spontaneous safety reports.
currentQuick:
Profhilo Body is an IBSA injectable hyaluronic acid product used by clinicians to treat skin laxity and roughness on areas like the upper arms and hands.
A 12-month single-arm study and a completed hands trial exist, but no controlled comparisons were found.
How it works: It uses hybrid complexes of high- and low-molecular-weight hyaluronic acid injected into the skin, intended to improve skin quality rather than add bulk.
Risks and caveats: A post-marketing review has assessed adverse event reports for the product family. Injection procedures carry general risks such as bruising and swelling, and it is given by trained clinicians.
deepLead:
Profhilo Body is an injectable hybrid hyaluronic acid (HA) product from IBSA Farmaceutici, marketed as a medical device for improving skin laxity and roughness on the body, such as the upper inner arms and the backs of the hands. It uses the NAHYCO hybrid technology, which forms cooperative complexes from high- and low-molecular-weight HA.
Published evidence includes a 12-month single-arm study of women with upper-arm skin laxity, a registered trial on the backs of the hands, and a post-marketing safety review of hybrid cooperative complex HA products used on the face and body. These are small and mostly uncontrolled.

name: Rejuran HB

angle.text: Rejuran HB is a polynucleotide skin booster used in aesthetic clinics to improve skin quality and texture. Published human data for this specific product are very limited.

summary: A polynucleotide skin-booster injectable with almost no published human data.
note: Only animal safety research found.
currentQuick:
Rejuran HB is a polynucleotide injectable used by clinicians as a skin booster.
The sources reviewed contain no human trials, only a rabbit study on accidental intra-arterial injection.
How it works: Polynucleotides are chains of nucleotides; skin booster products inject them into the skin. Specific mechanisms for Rejuran HB were not described in the sources reviewed.
Risks and caveats: The rabbit study examined vascular behaviour of polynucleotide products after intra-arterial exposure; human safety data were not found.
deepLead:
Rejuran HB is a polynucleotide (PN) injectable used in aesthetic medicine as a skin booster. Polynucleotides are chains of nucleotides, and the term covers DNA and RNA, which also have uses beyond cosmetics. Rejuran products are referred to in the literature as part of a family that includes Rejuran S and Rejuran HB Plus.
The only published study identified in the sources reviewed is an animal experiment on what happens when polynucleotide products are accidentally injected into an artery. No human clinical studies of Rejuran HB were found in those sources.

name: Juvelook

angle.text: Juvelook is a Korean PDLLA and hyaluronic acid biostimulator injected for tear troughs, folds and overall skin texture. Support comes from small studies and case reports.

summary: A Korean PDLLA-hyaluronic acid biostimulator injected for tear troughs, folds and skin texture, supported by small studies and case reports.
note: Nodule reports and animal data on intra-arterial injection exist.
currentQuick:
Juvelook is a poly-D,L-lactic acid injectable from VAIM Inc. in Korea, used by clinicians as a skin booster and collagen stimulator in areas such as under the eyes, nasolabial folds, forehead and cheeks.
Published evidence is mostly small studies, case series and case reports, mostly from 2025 and 2026.
How it works: PDLLA is described as a biostimulator that prompts the body to produce collagen over time. Some Juvelook variants are reported to combine PDLLA with hyaluronic acid.
Risks and caveats: Reported problems include firm nodules after tear trough injection. A rabbit study examined what happens with accidental intra-arterial injection. Procedures are performed by trained clinicians.
deepLead:
Juvelook is an injectable poly-D,L-lactic acid (PDLLA) product made by VAIM Inc. of Seoul, South Korea, used in aesthetic medicine as a skin booster and collagen-stimulating agent. Published reports describe a PDLLA and hyaluronic acid hybrid formulation, with variants named Juvelook Volume and Juvelook GLAM.
Published literature consists mainly of case reports, case series and small clinical studies, including use in the tear trough, nasolabial folds, forehead, sunken cheeks, clavicle and facial pores, as well as animal research and case reports of complications such as nodules.

name: Lenisna

angle.text: Lenisna is a PDLLA injectable used as a skin booster and collagen stimulator. Efficacy data for it are almost absent, and the main literature is a 2026 consensus on injection safety.

summary: A PDLLA booster with almost no published efficacy data; the main literature is a safety consensus on rare vision-loss complications.
note: Rare intravascular injection can cause visual impairment or blindness, per expert consensus.
currentQuick:
Lenisna is a poly-D,L-lactic acid injectable used in aesthetic clinics.
The only source found is an expert consensus on injection safety, not a trial of effectiveness.
How it works: PDLLA-HA products combine PDLLA microspheres, which stimulate collagen, with non-cross-linked hyaluronic acid as a carrier.
Risks and caveats: The consensus describes rare visual impairment and blindness after accidental injection into a blood vessel, and sets out management recommendations.
deepLead:
Lenisna is the name of a poly-D,L-lactic acid (PDLLA) injectable used in aesthetic medicine. The only source identified is a 2026 expert consensus on safe injection technique and the management of visual impairment caused by PDLLA-HA200, a next-generation injectable combining PDLLA microspheres with non-cross-linked hyaluronic acid as a carrier.
The consensus addresses a rare but serious complication, visual field impairment and blindness, that can result from inadvertent injection into a blood vessel. Efficacy studies of Lenisna were not found in the sources reviewed; the link between this consensus and the product name Lenisna is not established there beyond the PDLLA-HA200 class.

name: Aesthefill

angle.text: AestheFill is a Korean PDLLA microsphere biostimulator used to firm skin and soften lines gradually through collagen stimulation. Evidence includes one randomised trial against hyaluronic acid and many technique papers.

summary: A Korean PDLLA microsphere biostimulator with one randomised trial against hyaluronic acid and a large body of technique papers.
note: Clinician-prepared product; much literature concerns reconstitution technique.
currentQuick:
AestheFill is a PDLLA microsphere injectable from REGEN Biotech used by clinicians to restore facial volume and, increasingly, body contour.
A randomised, evaluator-blinded multicentre trial compared it with hyaluronic acid for nasolabial folds, and expert consensus papers address its preparation.
How it works: PDLLA microspheres in carboxymethyl cellulose are reconstituted and injected; the product is described as biostimulatory, prompting tissue to restore volume over time.
Risks and caveats: Technique-related issues such as lumping during reconstitution are discussed in the literature. Specific adverse event rates were not summarised in the sources reviewed. It is administered by trained clinicians.
deepLead:
AestheFill is an injectable poly-D,L-lactic acid (PDLLA) microsphere product made by REGEN Biotech of Seoul, South Korea. It contains PDLLA microspheres with carboxymethyl cellulose (CMC) as a suspending agent, supplied as a lyophilised powder that is reconstituted with sterile water before injection, and is described as biocompatible, biodegradable and biostimulatory.
It is used to correct soft-tissue volume loss in the face and, increasingly, the body. A randomised evaluator-blinded multicentre study compared it with hyaluronic acid for nasolabial fold augmentation. Much of the other literature concerns reconstitution methods and consensus technique recommendations.
